text.p: Britain's pace of economic growth quickened in the third quarter and looks set to accelerate next year, according to official figures published Friday.
Gross Domestic Product rose 2.3 percent in the third quarter from 2.2 percent in the second, suggesting the economy is enjoying more lively growth without igniting inflation.
The data pointed to more balanced economic growth, with manufacturing output starting to pick up, bolstering strong growth in the service sector.

"The figures show although the economy is growing at a strong pace there is no hint of a boom. They should give (finance minister Kenneth) Clarke enough leeway to leave rates on hold next week," said Andrew Cates, UK economist at UBS.
Clarke has cut interest rates four times since last December to the present 5.75 percent level and is under considerable political pressure to resist calls for a further increase.

Jeremy Hawkins, senior economic advisor at Bank America, agreed the Chancellor would use the GDP figures to argue for rates on hold. "The rise in GDP should constitute the final nail in the coffin of rate cut hopes, but it will certainly not be deemed strong enough by Clarke to justify a tightening."
The steady rise in GDP dispells any notion that growth is out of control and a 1980s type boom is brewing.

Other figures released on Friday showed the trade gap between Britain and the rest of the world improved dramatically in August, narrowing to 584 million sterling ($929.1 million) from 1.22 billion ($1.94 billion) in July.

Economists said it was too early to tell whether the recent rise in sterling was choking exports by making them "It's always difficult to work out how much is to do with appreciation and how much to do with weakness overseas. I think in this case it's more to do with slower growth overseas," especially in the U.S.," said Bank America's Jeremy Hawkins.
